text: And when I came to you, brothers, I did not come with lofty speech or wisdom as I proclaimed to you the testimony of God.

versions.text: And when I came to you, brothers, I did not come proclaiming God's testimony to you with lofty speech or wisdom.
versions.explanation: The current word order buries the contrast and repeats "to you" awkwardly close together ("proclaiming God's testimony to you with lofty speech"). Putting the negated phrase directly after "I did not come" follows the Greek order (οὐ καθʼ ὑπεροχὴν λόγου ἢ σοφίας) and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: For I resolved to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
And I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling,

versions.text: I came to you in weakness, in fear, and with much trembling,
versions.explanation: The initial κἀγὼ ("and I") links this clause to the preceding sentence and is currently dropped; ἐγενόμην πρὸς ὑμᾶς also emphasizes Paul's presence/state among them rather than merely the act of arriving. Keeping the parallel "in ... in ... in" preserves the Greek triad's rhythm for oral reading.

text: and my message and my preaching did not rest on persuasive words of wisdom, but on the demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God.
Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature—though not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing.
No, we speak God's wisdom, hidden in mystery, which God determined beforehand, before the ages, for our glory.
None of the rulers of this age understood it; for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
But as it is written: "What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, what has never entered the human heart—all that God has prepared for those who love him."
To us God has revealed it through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
For what human being knows a person's thoughts except that person's own spirit within him? In the same way, no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.

versions.text: For who among men knows a person's thoughts except that person's own spirit within him? In the same way, no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.
versions.explanation: "Who among men ... a person's ... that person's" mixes registers within one sentence. Rendering ἀνθρώπων consistently with the other occurrences of ἄνθρωπος makes the analogy clearer and smoother when read aloud.

text: And we have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know what God has freely given us.

This is what we speak—not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who have the Spirit.[^1]

[^1]: Or "expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words"; the Greek phrase can be understood either way.

versions.text: This is what we speak—not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who have the Spirit.
versions.explanation: The final clause is genuinely ambiguous in Greek (πνευματικοῖς can be masculine "spiritual people" or neuter "spiritual words/things"). A brief footnote alerts the reader to the alternative without changing the main text.

text: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; he cannot understand them, because they are discerned spiritually.
The spiritual person, however, discerns all things, while he himself is subject to no one's judgment.
For "who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?" But we have the mind of Christ.
